01 / EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS

Different questions.
Different kinds of evidence.

This analysis describes the people who answered the survey. It connects sample composition, independently rated threats, prompted impact selections, and brief written climate concerns.

Who can these results speak for? Recruitment used targeted, purposive snowball sampling through stakeholder organizations and project networks. This does not establish representativeness of the global public, national populations, or even everyone interested in climate change. The findings generate research and communication hypotheses; they do not establish policy priorities. Study methods ↗
QuestionWhat it measuresInterpretation boundary
Q7Independent severity ratings of marine/coastal threatsSeveral threats can receive equally high ratings; no forced ranking or resource allocation.
Q9Selection among specified marine/coastal climate impactsPrompted, multiple selections; distinct from general severity.
Q5Open-text climate concerns within respondents’ countriesIncludes terrestrial and social concerns; not exclusively marine.
Q12_10Agreement with benefits of solutions working with natural systemsSupplementary descriptive check; agreement does not establish willingness to volunteer.

Q10 addresses policy priorities more directly but is outside the notebook analysis presented here.

Q14–Q18 / SAMPLE COMPOSITION

Recreational users and highly educated respondents are prominent.

Tourists and recreational users account for 376 of 709 respondents (53.0%); conservation, management, and scientific respondents account for 233 (32.9%). Ages 18–40 represent 56.6%, while 18–30 alone represents 30.5%. These categories do not identify conventional college ages or recent graduates.

The five largest country groups—Italy, France, Ireland, the United Kingdom, and Spain—account for 554/709 (78.1%). The top ten account for 625/709 (88.2%). Their prominence shapes the overall pattern.

Q7 / PERCEIVED THREAT SEVERITY

Climate change and plastic pollution both receive high ratings.

Using high + very high as the comparison rule, climate change leads overall at 87.2%, followed by plastic pollution at 85.6%. Fishing/harvesting receives 77.2% and chemical pollution 72.5%; different pollution types should not be combined into one finding.

Respondent groupnClimate change: high + very highPlastic: high + very high

The metric changes the ordering. Plastic pollution leads on very high alone: 56.8%, versus 52.2% for climate change. Italy, France, and Spain rate plastic higher on the combined measure, but Spain rates climate change slightly higher on very-high-only ratings. These are sampled residents’ responses, not national opinion estimates.
Q9 × Q15 / SELECTED CLIMATE IMPACTS

Extreme weather, sea-level rise, and coastal erosion lead overall.

Respondents most often select changes in extreme-weather frequency (49.8%), sea-level rise (46.5%), and coastal erosion (39.9%). Sea-temperature change follows at 34.8%, and species-distribution change at 32.6%.

Include erosion in the story

Among conservation, management, and scientific respondents, coastal erosion (43.8%) slightly exceeds sea-level rise (43.3%). Both belong in the summary; biodiversity from Q5 is a different construct.

Small groups need careful interpretation

Fishing/seafood producers select species distribution and sea temperature at 8/14 each (57.1%). One person changes this group’s percentage by 7.1 points. This is an exploratory pattern, not a stable estimate for the sector.

Q5 / EXPLORATORY TEXT CODING

Broad climate concerns extend beyond the sea.

The notebook matches keywords in up to three answers per respondent, keeps answers separate during matching, and counts each person once per category. Of 709 respondents, 704 have retained nonempty text. This includes vague responses, place names, and expressions of no concern; it is not a count of validated, interpretable concerns.

Read these as keyword-category estimates. Categories overlap and differ in breadth. The chart’s original “themes” title is retained from the notebook, but the categories are not validated thematic findings. Sixteen retained respondents have no match; coverage does not establish coding accuracy.

Ecosystem loss is one recurring idea

“Loss of biodiversity”

Spreadsheet row 48 · Q5_1

This supports an ecosystem-loss interpretation. However, Q5 also includes terrestrial ecosystems; this category cannot be described wholesale as marine biodiversity concern.

Physical climate impacts are another

“Flooding”

Spreadsheet row 20 · Q5_1

This is a clear physical-impact example. The missed phrase “Warm days in winter” (row 404, Q5_1) shows that the keyword rules can overlook related concerns.

Documented audit: seven selected answer cells

This revision inspected seven answer cells from seven distinct respondent records, selected purposively to check known edge cases and clear positive matches. For each of the seven phrases below, the first exact occurrence was located by searching Q5_1, then Q5_2, then Q5_3 in original row order. This is a targeted answer-level audit, not a random review or a review of all answers from those respondents. Row references count the spreadsheet header as row 1. Excerpts retain the wording, with surrounding whitespace removed.

ReferenceExcerptOriginal keyword matchInterpretation / counterexample
Row 48 · Q5_1“Loss of biodiversity”Biodiversity & ecosystemsClear ecosystem concern; no evidence that it is specifically marine.
Row 20 · Q5_1“Flooding”FloodingClear positive example of a physical-impact concern.
Row 404 · Q5_1“Warm days in winter”No matchFalse negative for temperature concern.
Row 332 · Q5_3“Political Instability”Action, policy & adaptationSocial consequence; does not necessarily express a desired policy response.
Row 3 · Q5_2“Forest fires”Biodiversity & ecosystems; FiresOverlap needs an explicit rule; fire alone need not imply stated biodiversity loss.
Row 513 · Q5_1“Earthquake”Weather & disastersPossible climate-impact misattribution; preserve the perception without endorsing it.
Row 242 · Q5_1“Not concerned”No matchCounterexample to assuming every retained answer expresses a concern; other answers in the record may differ.

The audit demonstrates specific errors and ambiguity; it cannot estimate precision or recall. An answer’s match here is not necessarily its respondent’s complete set of matches across all three answers. No claim about within-country consistency is made without country-level text summaries.

Proposed coding rules and next validation step
  • Temperature: include explicit warming, unusual warmth, or temperature change; add “warm days in winter.” Exclude unspecified “change.”
  • Ecosystems: include explicit species, habitat, or biodiversity harm. Code forest fires as fires; add ecosystems only when ecological harm is explicit. Marine and terrestrial references should be distinguished.
  • Action/policy: include explicit mitigation, adaptation, or governance responses; move political instability to social consequences unless the answer also proposes a policy.
  • Hazards: retain flood, fire, and other hazard labels separately; flag geological hazards as possible attribution uncertainty, not established climate mechanisms.
  • No concern / insufficient detail: keep explicit “not concerned” separate from vague terms, place names, and missing answers.

These are proposed revisions, not applied recoding. Before updating totals, independently review a documented random sample of matched and unmatched answers, resolve disagreements, and record changes to the codebook. The seven selected examples are diagnostic and not an accuracy estimate.

Supplementary word cloud

Word frequency is an illustration, not an interpretation or a validated theme count.

Within this sample, climate change and plastic pollution both attract strong severity ratings. Extreme weather, sea-level rise, and erosion are frequently selected impacts. Written answers broaden the picture—but require better coding before stronger thematic conclusions are justified.

03 / POTENTIAL A/B TEST

Can a message turn
interest into participation?

Proposed study · not conducted. An Italian coastal-restoration campaign could test whether ecosystem or community framing changes completed volunteer registrations. This tests communication, not restoration effectiveness or underlying priorities.

Why this experiment? A supplementary check of Q12_10 finds 679/709 respondents (95.8%) agree or strongly agree that solutions working with natural systems can improve ecosystems and benefit people. This descriptive check was added for the website revision; it is not an original notebook finding, an Italy-specific estimate, or evidence of readiness to volunteer.

Hypothesis: A community-framed headline increases completed registrations compared with an ecosystem-framed headline among eligible visitors to an Italian coastal-restoration campaign.

A / Ecosystem framing

Restore the coast for its ecosystems.

Join a local coastal-restoration volunteer day. Read the project details, activities, and participation requirements, then reserve a place.

Register for a volunteer day

B / Community framing

Restore the coast for its communities.

Join a local coastal-restoration volunteer day. Read the project details, activities, and participation requirements, then reserve a place.

Register for a volunteer day

Illustrative English copy for an Italian campaign. Final Italian wording would be checked for equivalent meaning before launch. Only the framing in the headline changes; body copy, verified project facts, images, CTA, form, and placement remain identical. These are previews, not active signup buttons.

Audience & assignment

Recruit adults eligible to attend one partner’s coastal-restoration events in a defined Italian service area. Keep recruitment channels and geographic eligibility fixed. Randomize eligible unique visitors 1:1 on first exposure and preserve their assigned version.

One primary outcome

Completed, deduplicated volunteer registrations within seven days of first exposure, divided by all eligible visitors assigned to each arm. Analyze by original assignment. Attendance at the event is a secondary follow-through measure; clicks are diagnostic.

Sample size & timing

Use a separate pilot to estimate baseline registration, then calculate the required sample for a two-sided 5% significance level and 80% power. Prespecify sample size and a fixed recruitment window before launch, with seven additional days for outcome collection. Do not stop early after a promising result.

Meaningful improvement and decision rule

As a planning target, define a worthwhile improvement as 20% relative to the pilot baseline, subject to the partner’s capacity and costs. A rise from 25% to 30% is 20% relative improvement and 5 percentage points. A rise from 25% to 45% is 20 percentage points. These are illustrative values, not observed conversion rates.

Report both registration rates, the absolute difference (B − A), relative lift, and a 95% confidence interval. Adopt B only if the confidence interval’s lower bound exceeds the prespecified worthwhile absolute improvement; favor A under the symmetric rule. Otherwise report the result as inconclusive for a practically meaningful winner. Because this rule is stricter than merely excluding zero, the final power analysis must evaluate the probability of meeting this decision rule under a specified expected effect.

Document bot and duplicate exclusions before assignment, missing outcome handling, campaign capacity, and technical checks. Keep demographic interactions exploratory unless separately planned and powered. Differences in treatment response may indicate variation in effectiveness; they are not automatically sampling bias.

A positive result supports a particular message for the tested audience and setting. It does not show that restoration is effective, identify which bundled benefits people value most, or establish public policy preferences. This portfolio does not randomize visitors or collect experiment data.

What changed after critique

The question now concerns survey respondents rather than worldwide priorities. Severity ratings, prompted impact selections, and national open-text concerns are interpreted separately. The five-country share is corrected to 78.1%; Spain’s threat comparison and coastal erosion are included.

Original keyword counts are retained with explicit limitations and a seven-answer audit. The A/B proposal isolates framing and specifies actual registration as its primary outcome. No inferential claims or experimental results are presented.

AI use disclosure: ChatGPT and Gemini were utilized to assist with coding and visualizations.
